name: Omar Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time, Omar. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say is confidential, so you can tell me both your public line and what you really think. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: These days it's mostly new connections out on the plains. Every second farmer wants a solar field or a couple of wind turbines, and somebody has to build the line to bring that power into the grid, and that's my crew. We're out by seven, set poles, string conductor, and I spend half my day on the phone with the farmer, the contractor and the control room. I like building something new, honestly, instead of only patching old stuff. What wears me out is the heat in summer: there's no shade out there, not one tree.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How does technology show up in your day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Everywhere, and I like it. I plan the week with an AI assistant, I use it to check pole loadings and to write the reports the office wants. I got my drone licence last year on my own time, so I fly the route before we start and save us a day of walking. The guys call me the professor, but they ask me to fly it every time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let me read you five pictures of the future, one at a time. This one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, it's still a decent tool, it just didn't change the world. I'd keep using it and telling the younger guys to use it. I'm not someone who posts much, but I might send my son a joke about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I carry on, which is fine. My job's busy because of all the solar and wind, and that doesn't depend on AI. My real headache is the debt we've still got.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working, keep using the tools I use now. Pay down the loan as fast as I can, maybe take more weekend work. Keep flying the drone for the crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit underwhelmed, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned debt. What's behind that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three years ago my son Rui and I started a food truck, tacos and grilled corn at the farm markets. It went well for one summer and then it didn't, and we sold the truck for less than we owed. I'm still paying off my share, so there's never more than a month of money in the account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still do anything with the drone in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. I've thought about doing inspections for the solar farms on weekends. It's not a big idea, but it'd help with the loan.

S0.say: I'd say it's still a decent tool that just didn't change the world. I'd keep using it and encourage the younger crew to as well.
S0.think: Privately I carry on, and my job is busy because of solar and wind, not AI. My real headache is the debt we still have.
S0.do: Keeps working and using the same tools, and pays down his loan as fast as he can with extra weekend work. Considers weekend drone inspections for solar farms.
S0.quote: It went well for one summer and then it didn't, and we sold the truck for less than we owed.
S0.fieldNote: Omar is a busy, tech-friendly crew leader whose work is driven by new solar and wind links. His thin savings come from a failed food truck with his son. He's a risk-taker even outside work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is going to change how we work, so let's get good at it early. At work I'd be showing people the tools and telling them not to be scared of it. I'd say it in a practical way, not a big speech.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd do fine, maybe better than fine. I already use the stuff every day, and I've got a drone licence most of my crew don't have. They'll need people who can run the machines and still know the lines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get on any course for line robots or drone stringing straight away, in the first few months. I'd start the weekend drone inspection side business, small, maybe two jobs a month to start. And I'd keep paying off the loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Interested, even a little excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd start the inspection business. Is that realistic with your money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a risk, I know, after the food truck. But the drone's already mine, and the only cost is insurance and my weekends. Ines would make me promise not to borrow anything this time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about this change you'd worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The older guys, like Bruno, who's 63 and hates screens. And I'd worry the company uses it to cut crews rather than make us faster. But that's for management and the union to sort out.

S1.say: I'd say it's going to change how we work, so let's get good at it early. At work I'd show people the tools and tell them not to be scared.
S1.think: Privately I think I'd do fine, maybe better, since I use the tools daily and hold a drone licence. They'll need people who run the machines and know the lines.
S1.do: Signs up for line robot and drone stringing courses in the first months. Starts a small weekend drone inspection business with two jobs a month and keeps paying off the loan.
S1.feel: Calm, interested and a little excited.
S1.quote: Ines would make me promise not to borrow anything this time.
S1.fieldNote: Steady disruption looks like an opportunity to him. He's aware of the food truck failure and keeps the new idea small and cheap. He's pragmatic about crew cuts, leaving it to management and the union.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now three pictures about full AGI, at different speeds. This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast and we need some brakes on it, from government and companies both. At work I'd tell people to grab whatever training they can and not wait. I'd be practical, but I'd be worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means trouble. I'd be 60, with a loan still running and about a month of money. Even with my skills, a full AGI with robots doesn't need a professor with a drone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to get onto whatever team manages the robots at the company, the first week it exists. I'd cut back on everything at home and push the loan down. I'd look for any work that pays, even outside the grid, like supervising solar farm robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. My stomach drops a bit, but I'd be busy, not frozen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the side business if robots can do inspections too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It probably dies before it starts, honestly. In two years the AI flies the drone and writes the report itself. I'd drop it and put everything into keeping a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the conversation at home that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ines would say, we'll manage, and she'd mean it, because teachers might last a bit longer. I'd say, we'll manage, and I'd be less sure. Then we'd go through the budget at the kitchen table until midnight.

S2.say: I'd say it's too fast and needs brakes from both government and companies. At work I'd tell people to grab any training now.
S2.think: Privately it means trouble at 60, with a loan running and about a month of money. Even with my skills, full AGI with robots doesn't need a professor with a drone.
S2.do: Tries to join the company's robot management team the first week it exists. Cuts back at home, pushes down the loan, drops the side business and looks for any paid work, including supervising solar farm robots.
S2.feel: Anxious, with his stomach dropping, but busy rather than frozen.
S2.quote: Even with my skills, a full AGI with robots doesn't need a professor with a drone.
S2.fieldNote: His adaptability keeps him moving even under a fast shock. He drops the side business quickly because he sees it won't hold. The thin savings and old loan are what turn this from an opportunity into a threat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is short, but we can work with it. I'd tell the company to start training now and I'd tell the guys to get on board. I'd say it more hopefully than the fast one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd make it. In five years I'd be 63, and I could be running robot crews by then and retire a couple of years later. If the loan's gone, the money gap is manageable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd get qualified in robot supervision and ask to lead a trial crew. I'd grow the drone side business for two or three years, while it's still useful, and put the money into the loan. Once the loan's gone, I'd start saving properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a way I can handle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the first concrete step?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ask my supervisor for a meeting and say: when the robots come, I want to be the one running them. Then sign up for the course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change anything for your kids?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Rui to stop thinking about food trucks and think about what people will still pay a person for. Sofia's a nurse, so she'd probably be okay. I'd keep the family plans as they are.

S3.say: I'd say five years is short but workable. I'd tell the company to start training now and the crew to get on board.
S3.think: Privately I think I'd make it, running robot crews by 63 and retiring a couple of years later. Once the loan is gone, the money gap is manageable.
S3.do: Gets qualified in robot supervision in the first year and asks to lead a trial crew. Grows the drone side business for two or three years to pay off the loan, then starts saving properly.
S3.quote: When the robots come, I want to be the one running them.
S3.fieldNote: Five years turns his scramble into a plan he believes in. The side business has a set lifespan in his mind. He's practical and specific about the first step.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, if we use it. I'd push the company to make a training plan and show the young guys there's a path. I'd be pretty upbeat about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm in good shape in this one. I'd be retired before it fully lands, and I'd have time to clear the loan and build something. I'd maybe even enjoy the change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and learn every new tool as it comes. I'd grow the drone inspection business over a few years, maybe buy a second drone. And I'd clear the debt and start saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Even looking forward to some of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be 68 by then. Does ten years feel safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty safe, yes. I'd be retired at 65 or 66, and I'd have time to make the side business pay for itself. The young guys have more to worry about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you put any money into the drone business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, once the loan's gone, maybe a second drone with a thermal camera, a couple of thousand. I'd wait until I had the jobs lined up, though. I learned that from the food truck.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a gift if we use it. I'd push the company for a training plan and show young workers there's a path.
S4.think: Privately I'm in good shape, retiring before it lands with time to clear the loan and build something. I might even enjoy the change.
S4.do: Keeps working and learns new tools as they arrive. Clears the debt, starts saving and grows the drone business, buying a second drone with a thermal camera once jobs are lined up.
S4.feel: Calm, even looking forward to some of it.
S4.quote: I'd wait until I had the jobs lined up, though. I learned that from the food truck.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years he's calm and even keen. His caution about investing is a lesson from the food truck. He sees the risk falling on younger workers rather than himself.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I'd be 60 with the loan still running and about a month of money, and even my drone wouldn't save me. What would help is the company giving older guys first chance at the robot jobs, and some help for people with debt while they switch.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what the robots are building. If they're building all these solar lines faster, the farmers are happy, the bills might go down. It's not all bad, it's the speed and who gets the money.

headlineQuote: It's not all bad, it's the speed and who gets the money.
portrait: Omar Silva is a 58-year-old crew leader building new grid connections for solar and wind farms on the plains, a tech fan who plans with AI and flies his own drone. A failed food truck with his son left him with a loan and about a month of savings. He's calm about a plateau and steady change, keen to learn robots and start a small drone inspection business. Fast AGI makes him anxious because of the debt, though he keeps moving rather than freezing. With five or ten years he sees himself running robot crews and building the side business, and he grows hopeful.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because he'd be 60 with his loan still running and about a month of money.
whatWouldHelp: The company giving older workers first chance at robot jobs, and help for people with debt while they switch.
